item.text: {"question_id":"8B.7","answer":"Progress toward Scholz’s frozen goals was mixed and only partly attributable to his government. Energy-crisis management plausibly limited a deeper downturn: independent DIW modeling estimated that relief measures supported consumption, with stronger support for lower-income households, although the distributional effect was mixed and the estimate was model-based. Energy security also improved through LNG, storage, and relief measures, but the strongest implementation claims came from Scholz’s own speeches. Ukraine-support commitments and deployments were substantial, yet defense readiness, spending adequacy, and the conversion of commitments into durable capability remained contested against a heavily inherited baseline. Broader economic and distributional outcomes were uneven: 2023 GDP fell 0.3%, private consumption and construction weakened, while employment and some lower-quintile effective wages improved. Poverty-risk and social-exclusion indicators were broadly unchanged, but the 2023 income measures partly refer to 2022 income and included preliminary results. Family-reunification visas exceeded the annual quota, although Afghan admission implementation remained delayed and contested. Russia’s war, energy prices, inflation, interest rates, ECB policy, global demand, private-sector decisions, inherited administrative and defense weaknesses, and coalition/institutional constraints limit causal attribution. The evidence therefore supports some crisis-response progress, but not a clear net advance across the broader portfolio by the end of the 2023 observation
